sections.label: The opening
sections.line: The views worked; readers now need to choose them
sections.para: Five reader agents produced a catalogue, maps, an arc, a two-minute version and a deck, but they arrived as one mixed fold under the abstract. Now the reader picks a way in with one tap in the pane, mostly computed deterministically, a local model for the rest, and the finished article kept whole.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Readers pick the way in; the article stays central
sections.para: The pane offers headlines, infographic, two minutes, slides, what is new, facts, relationships, vocabulary and the whole article, with a default per persona and the mode in the address. Most modes are deterministic projections; a browser model handles the rest. What is new needs the vault, and phone and email come first.

sections.label: Focus and time
sections.line: A reader's constraint is time, and their need focus
sections.para: Long articles are where the thinking and evidence live, and the answer was never shorter ones. The same person reads everything on Sunday and headlines on Tuesday, and an article can be two minutes or an hour depending on what was read before. The unit of choice is the way in, chosen at the piece.

sections.label: The modes
sections.line: Ten ways in, most built from existing views
sections.para: Headlines, the infographic, two minutes, the slides, facts, relationships and vocabulary come from existing views and structure. What is new crosses the Historian's arc with the reader's vault records, and is the default I would choose. At my level, for my persona needs a model in the reader's tab, and the whole article remains.

sections.label: Deterministic first, a model second
sections.line: Deterministic modes first; a local model fits the rest
sections.para: Modes built from checked views are projections: computed, explainable, identical for every reader, free and testable by script. Only fitting the article to a reader's level, persona or question needs a model, and that should run locally. Chrome's Prompt API ships but is rough, which matters little because deterministic modes carry most value.

sections.label: What the article keeps that the graph loses
sections.line: The finished article keeps the narrative a graph loses
sections.para: It is tempting to treat the article as disposable, regenerated from the graph, but a finished article has a beginning, pacing, surprise and voice. The graph is right for provenance and zooming but carries nobody anywhere. The modes are ways in, not replacements, and the site will now say finished article, not prose.

sections.label: The brief
sections.line: The brief: modes in the pane, the fold removed
sections.para: For the newsroom session, written 12 October 2026: a row of modes in the pane replaces the fold, with a default per persona and the mode in the address. Computed modes come first, what is new starts with local storage, the phone gets a bottom sheet, email follows the default, and each mode gets an experiment.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Views exist for five articles; model modes must wait
sections.para: Modes built from the five readers' views come first for those five articles, while the rest of the site supports graph and figure modes. Local browser models are rough and the design does not depend on them. What is new needs reading records, and whether a default changes reading is an experiment tested first on me.
